_README: TEMPLATE CONFIG. Replace every value containing 'FILL:' before your first real run -- `./check-setup.sh` lists what is still unfilled, and jobscan.py refuses to run a scan while any remain. A worked, fully-filled and verified version of this file is in examples/config.json. Structure: each source has a `kind` (which platform to talk to). A source with `group: discovery` draws on max_discovery and faces the stricter discovery_* prescreen. See PLATFORMS.md for the platform reference; /jobscan-connector adds a company for you.

companies._README: ONE OF TWO SOURCES THAT WORK FOR ANYBODY, and the only two shipped in this template. This is a company-less sweep across every employer The Muse indexes in your regions -- no key, no credentials, full descriptions (~4k chars). It is how employers you had never heard of reach your shortlist, and it is worth keeping whatever field you are in. Add your own tracked companies alongside it (/jobscan-connector); they draw on a separate budget, so a broad sweep can never starve the boards you deliberately chose. CATEGORY NAMES MUST MATCH THE MUSE EXACTLY -- a wrong one silently returns 0 while --check still prints `ok`. Verified 2026-08-24: 'Science and Engineering', 'Business Operations', 'Data and Analytics', 'Software Engineering', 'Healthcare', 'Product Management' all return results; 'Operations' and 'Engineering' return 0 because they are not real category names.
locations: FILL: city, ST -- one entry per city you would work in, e.g. 'Boston, MA'
FILL: another city, or delete this line
categories: FILL: a real Muse category name -- see _README above for verified ones

companies._README: THE SECOND UNIVERSAL SOURCE. Remote-only aggregator, ~108k roles, no key, full descriptions (~4.9k chars median). It does NOT duplicate The Muse: metro aggregators index employers against offices, so remote-first companies -- which have no office -- never appear there at all. Multi-employer, hence group:discovery. SET `queries` AND IT USES THE FILTERED SEARCH ENDPOINT, which is the difference between this source earning its place and not. Measured on the same budget: browse firehose (no queries) gave 400 fetched -> 1 past the prescreen, because the raw feed is overwhelmingly remote sales and support; eight keyword queries gave 283 fetched -> 60 past the prescreen. `q` IS FUZZY AND MORE WORDS BROADEN RATHER THAN NARROW -- q=engineer returns 31 hits while q=mechanical engineer returns 147 -- so write specific role phrases, not one broad word. Rows are deduped across queries. Cost is one request per 20 rows (queries x pages). Optional: `seniority` (Entry-level|Mid-level|Senior|Manager|Director|Executive -- note `Senior`, NOT `Senior-level`, which returns HTTP 400), `employment_type`, `exclude_worldwide`. `country` accepts US / USA / us / 'United States' and INCLUDES worldwide-eligible roles unless you pass exclude_worldwide. DELETE THIS SOURCE if you will not take a remote job -- every row it returns is remote.
queries: FILL: a specific role phrase, e.g. 'mechanical engineer' -- see _README
FILL: another phrase, or delete this line

_companies_examples._README: NOT USED BY THE TOOL -- reference only. Copy an entry into `companies` above and fill in the identifiers. Each `kind` needs different ones; PLATFORMS.md maps a careers URL to its kind, and /jobscan-connector works this out for a company and verifies it. TOKENS ARE NOT GUESSABLE and are case-sensitive: one real board is `thriveMarket`, and a company's Greenhouse token was `<name>-careers` after three obvious guesses 404'd. Search, do not guess.

smartrecruiters._warning: Returns HTTP 200 with totalFound=0 for an UNKNOWN token instead of 404, so status code alone can never validate this source. Check the count against what the careers page shows.

workday._warning: A 422 means the tenant resolved but the site slug is wrong. Take the slug from the real careers URL: tenant.wdN.myworkdayjobs.com/SITE.

locations: one city per region -- location is radius-based and NOT repeatable

themuse_company.company_query: Employer Name As Muse Spells It
themuse_company._warning: For employers whose own portal resists scripting. Omit `categories` unless you have confirmed that employer's postings actually carry them -- see the silent-zero note in PLATFORMS.md.

himalayas._warning: Remote-only, no key, full descriptions. MUST be group:discovery (multi-employer). Always set `queries` -- without them it falls back to an unfiltered newest-first feed whose yield is near zero.

clearcompany._warning: Get site_id from the careers page: <script src=https://careers-content.clearcompany.com/js/v1/career-site.js?siteId=UUID>. That tag's src may be UNQUOTED, so grep the raw HTML for `clearcompany` rather than matching src="...". Locations come back as 'City ST' with no comma -- make sure regions.wanted has a bare ' st' form or every role is silently dropped.

prescreen._README: Title-level gate, applied before the LLM scoring pass -- cheap, and it keeps the scoring payload small. A title is rejected if it matches anything in `block`; it then needs at least `min_signal` hits from `signal`. Discovery rows must ADDITIONALLY clear `discovery_block` and match `discovery_signal`, because an open sweep is mostly roles with nothing to do with you, while a company you deliberately tracked deserves the benefit of the doubt on a weak title. EXPECT TO RETUNE THESE FOR MONTHS. The Skip-reasons in your shortlist are the feedback loop (see SCORING.md). The rule of thumb: when noise gets through, TIGHTEN `block` rather than narrowing `signal` -- narrowing `signal` drops real roles silently, while a bad block term shows up the moment you look for a title you expected. `block` entries are regexes (case-insensitive); `signal` entries are plain lowercase substrings.
block: FILL: add the noise categories specific to your field and your boards -- see _block_README
prescreen._block_README: The entries shipped above are the universal ones: wrong function (sales, legal, HR), wrong level (intern, new grad, director, VP), and management tracks. They apply to almost any search -- keep them unless you actually want those roles, and delete `director`/`vice president` if you are senior enough to. Note the anchors: `\bintern\b` rather than `intern$`, because 'Robotics Intern - Real-Time Controls' does not end with the word; and `manager of` alongside `manager,` for the same reason. Anchoring bugs are the most common way a block list quietly under-performs. What you must ADD is the noise your own boards produce. Two real examples: a university board was ~85% clinical postings and 'Clinical Lab Scientist' matched the `scientist` signal; an open sweep in an energy-and-finance-heavy state produced a wall of oilfield and insurance titles. You cannot predict these -- run once, read candidates.md, then add. AND BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU BLOCK: one over-broad term silently kills roles you want. `radiolog` was deliberately NOT blocked on that clinical board because it would also have blocked medical-imaging ML research. THE RULE THAT OVERRIDES 'JUST TIGHTEN BLOCK': never block a LEARNABLE gap. A `block` term deletes a role before anyone reads it, while a gap in profile.md is merely weighed against the rest of the posting -- these are different mechanisms and confusing them is the most damaging mistake you can make here. Block HARD GATES only (an active clearance, a licence, work authorization -- things that make the role unobtainable however good the fit). Never block the name of a tool or technology the candidate would learn: the same technology appears in jobs that are otherwise nothing alike, so weigh the surrounding domain instead. A real case: adding `gpu` to a block list looked sensible and would have discarded the highest-scoring role that search ever produced. Ask of every candidate term: is this unobtainable, or merely unfamiliar?
signal: FILL: the terms that make a TITLE worth reading in your field -- 20-30 of them, lowercase substrings
FILL: include the obvious ones and their abbreviations, e.g. both 'machine learning' and 'ml '
FILL: include role-shape words as well as domain words, e.g. 'research engineer', 'scientist'
prescreen._caps_README: max_to_score caps tracked candidates, max_discovery caps discovery ones, and they are SEPARATE on purpose: sharing one budget let a broad sweep across 50 employers starve the boards you chose. Both discovery sources shipped above share max_discovery, which is the point. All caps are filled round-robin across companies, so one large board cannot crowd out a small one -- a global sort once let a 600-role board bury an 8-role one entirely.
discovery_signal: FILL: the STRICTER list for open search -- only the terms that alone justify reading an unknown employer's posting
FILL: usually a subset of `signal` with the generic words removed
discovery_block: FILL: what an open sweep floods you with in your field

_manual._README: Companies with no automated route, and what covers them instead. Record WHAT WAS TRIED -- the exact endpoints and how they failed -- not 'doesn't work'. A negative verdict is only as good as the specific thing that was tried, and two portals in this project's history sat here as 'nothing works' for an entire session before a re-test found a route that had been there all along. When one of these starts mattering, run /jobscan-connector and make it re-derive the verdict from scratch. The realistic fallback for a genuinely closed portal is a saved-search email alert on the company's own site.
FILL: e.g. 'BrassRing (partnerid=NNNNN). ProcessSortAndShowMoreJobs answers but returns a fixed 3 featured jobs with Total=0; the documented MatchedJobs endpoint 500s even with a session cookie. Not on The Muse. NO ROUTE.'

_filter_locations_README: true keeps only roles whose location matches `regions.wanted` above; false disables location filtering entirely and scores everything the prescreen passes.

regions._README: Region tokens for the location filter, matched case-insensitively against whatever a feed calls the location. THIS IS THE SECOND MOST PERSONAL THING IN THIS FILE after the prescreen. Include: your state's name; its abbreviation in several punctuation forms (', ma' / 'ma,' / ' ma ') because feeds disagree -- 'US, MA, Boston', 'Boston, MA' and 'Boston, Massachusetts' all occur; and every city you would actually work in. Keep 'remote' if you would take a remote job. WATCH FOR CITY-NAME COLLISIONS: a bare 'portland' matches both Oregon and Maine, and Pasadena, Springfield, Columbus, Kansas City and Charleston all exist in more than one state -- qualify them ('portland, or'). `foreign` and `ambiguous` are optional: omit them and jobscan.py falls back to DEFAULT_FOREIGN (a generic list of non-US place names) and DEFAULT_AMBIGUOUS ('locations', 'multiple', 'various' -- the vague strings Workday uses instead of listing sites). Override `foreign` if you are searching outside the US.
wanted: FILL: 'remote' if you would take one, then your state, its abbreviations, and your cities
